stem: Jonas asks Mira what makes `root` different from the other accounts on the studio’s Linux machines. Which answer is correct?
explanation: Root is the superuser account with user ID 0. Because the kernel skips the usual permission checks for UID 0, a typo as root can wreck the system, which is why you work as a standard user and borrow root’s rights only when needed.

options.text: The name `root` is what the kernel checks, so any account with another name and UID 0 would be an ordinary user.
options.rationale: The kernel looks at the number, not the name: an account with UID 0 is root whatever it is called.

options.text: Its user ID is 0, and permission checks do not restrict it, so it can read, change and delete any file.
options.rationale: Root is defined by UID 0, not by its name; the kernel lets that user ID bypass the normal permission checks.

options.text: It is the first account created at install time and therefore holds the lowest user ID above 1000, the standard start.
options.rationale: Root’s ID is 0, and the first standard user gets 1000 on Debian.

options.text: It is simply a member of the group `sudo`, which grants extra rights to every user inside it.
options.rationale: Membership of `sudo` only allows running commands through `sudo`; it does not make an account root.

stem: Ada opens a root shell on the build machine to look around. Where does root’s home directory live?
explanation: Root’s home directory is `/root`. A root shell usually ends its prompt with `#`, where a standard user’s ends with `$`.

options.text: `/home/root`
options.rationale: Standard users live under `/home`, but root’s home is the separate top-level `/root`.
The prompt may start in `/` for some tools, but root’s home directory is `/root`.

options.text: `/var/root`
options.rationale: `/var` holds variable data such as logs; root’s home is not there.

options.text: `/root`
options.rationale: Root’s home is `/root`, so it stays reachable even if `/home` is on a separate disk that is not mounted.

stem: Why does the studio tell its staff to work as standard users instead of logging in as root all day?
explanation: Working with the least rights you need is a core security habit. You then borrow root’s power for single commands with `sudo`, so mistakes stay small and the log shows who did what.

options.text: A mistake or a malicious program then can only damage what that standard user is allowed to change.
options.rationale: Limited rights limit the damage: a bad `rm` or a malware download cannot reach the system files.

options.text: Standard users run commands faster because the kernel does not check permissions for them.
options.rationale: It is the other way round: root skips permission checks, standard users are checked on every access.

options.text: Root cannot start graphical programs, so a standard user is the only option for the desktop.
options.rationale: Root can run any program; the reason is safety, not capability.

options.text: Linux allows only one root session at a time, so the standard accounts avoid waiting for it.
options.rationale: Nothing limits the number of root sessions; the point is to keep the rights small.

stem: Mira needs to confirm that the password hashes are not readable by every standard user. Which file stores them, and who may read it?
explanation: The user database is split in two so that programs can look up names and IDs without seeing secrets: `/etc/passwd` is world-readable, while the password hashes sit in `/etc/shadow`.

options.text: `/etc/passwd`, which only root may read.
options.rationale: Every user can read `/etc/passwd`, and it holds only an `x` in the password field.

options.text: `/etc/group`, which only the group `sudo` may read.
options.rationale: `/etc/group` lists groups and their members and is world-readable.

options.text: `/etc/shadow`, which only root (and the group `shadow`) may read.
options.rationale: `/etc/shadow` holds the hashes and is deliberately closed to ordinary users.

options.text: `/etc/skel`, which only the file’s owner may read.
options.rationale: `/etc/skel` is the template directory copied into new home directories.

stem: Before restarting the build machine, Ada wants to see who is logged in right now and what each of them is running. Which command shows that?
explanation: `who` and `w` report who is logged in now, and `w` adds what each user is doing. `last` reads the login history, and `id` or `groups` describe one account’s IDs and groups.

options.text: `id`
options.rationale: `id` prints the user and group IDs of one account, not a list of sessions.

options.text: `last`
options.rationale: `last` shows the history of past logins, not what is running now.
`w` lists the logged-in users, their terminals and the command each one is running.

options.text: `groups`
options.rationale: `groups` lists the group names of an account.

stem: Which of these /etc/passwd lines describes a system user, as the studio’s web server would use?
explanation: System users belong to services. They have low IDs (below 1000 on Debian), usually no password and a shell such as `/usr/sbin/nologin` so nobody can log in as them.

options.text: `www-data:x:33:33:www-data:/var/www:/usr/sbin/nologin`
options.rationale: The UID is below 1000 and the shell is `/usr/sbin/nologin`, the typical marks of a service account.

options.text: `ada:x:1002:1002:Ada Lindqvist:/home/ada:/bin/bash`
options.rationale: UID 1002 and a real shell make this a standard user.

options.text: `jonas:x:1001:1001:Jonas Berg:/home/jonas:/bin/bash`
options.rationale: This is Jonas’s standard account with UID 1001.

options.text: `mira:x:1000:1000:Mira Okafor:/home/mira:/bin/bash`
options.rationale: UID 1000 is the first standard user on Debian.

stem: The studio’s web server runs as `www-data` instead of root. What is the main security benefit?
explanation: Giving each service its own low-privilege account is called privilege separation. A flaw in the service only exposes what that account may touch.

options.text: The account is protected by a longer password than any standard user would use.
options.rationale: System users usually have no password at all.

options.text: Root cannot read files that belong to a system user, so they stay private.
options.rationale: Root can read everything, whoever owns it.

options.text: The web server then runs faster, because system users skip the log-in checks.
options.rationale: Running as another user has no effect on speed; the point is limiting damage.

options.text: If the web server is hacked, the attacker only gets the few rights of that service account.
options.rationale: The service account owns almost nothing, so a compromise stays contained.

stem: On a Debian system, which user ID range is normally used for system users such as `daemon` and `www-data`?
explanation: Debian Policy puts system users below 1000 (IDs 100–999 are handed out as software is installed) and standard users from 1000. The limit is configured by `UID_MIN` in `/etc/login.defs`, and other distributions can differ.

options.text: 1000 to 59999, the range reserved for the services that run on the machine.
options.rationale: That range is where standard users begin on Debian.

options.text: Below 1000, apart from 0 (root).
options.rationale: Debian reserves IDs 1–999 for system accounts and starts standard users at 1000.

options.text: Exactly 0, because every service must run with root’s ID and rights.
options.rationale: Only root has UID 0; services get their own IDs.

options.text: Above 60000, so that they can never clash with the accounts of the studio’s people.
options.rationale: System accounts use the low numbers; the very high ones are for special accounts such as `nobody`.

stem: Mira finds that the account `daemon` has `/usr/sbin/nologin` as its shell. What does that mean?
explanation: Service accounts exist so that files and processes can be owned by something other than root. Setting the shell to `nologin` makes sure nobody uses them as a normal login.

options.text: The account is locked and its password has been removed from `/etc/shadow` by the administrator.
options.rationale: Locking an account is done in `/etc/shadow` with `passwd -l`; the shell field has nothing to do with it.

options.text: The account may only log in over SSH, never at the console.
options.rationale: `nologin` blocks interactive sessions altogether, including over SSH.

options.text: The account can log in but every command is recorded for the administrators.
options.rationale: No session is started at all, so no commands can be recorded.

options.text: Nobody can open an interactive session as that account; the shell just prints a refusal.
options.rationale: `nologin` is a stand-in shell that denies interactive logins while the account still owns files and processes.

stem: Mira runs `sudo apt update` and is asked for a password. Whose password does `sudo` expect?
explanation: `sudo` asks for your own password and then consults `/etc/sudoers` to see whether you may run the command as root. `su` asks for the target account’s password.

options.text: The root password, the same one that `su` would ask for.
options.rationale: That is `su` behaviour; `sudo` does not need the root password.

options.text: Her own, since `sudo` checks that she is allowed to run the command as root.
options.rationale: `sudo` authenticates the caller with the caller’s own password.

options.text: The password of the first user on the machine.
options.rationale: There is no such rule; `sudo` asks the user who typed the command.

options.text: No password at all: every member of `sudo` can run commands without asking.
options.rationale: By default a password is required; only a specific sudoers entry can drop that.

stem: Jonas types `su - ada`. What does the dash do?
explanation: With `su - NAME` you get a login shell: the environment variables, working directory and settings of the target account. Plain `su NAME` keeps most of your current environment. `exit` returns you.

options.text: It tells `su` to ask for Jonas’s own password instead of Ada’s.
options.rationale: `su` always asks for the password of the account you switch to; the dash does not change that.

options.text: It runs a single command and then returns to Jonas’s shell.
options.rationale: Running one command is `-c`; the dash selects a login shell.

options.text: It starts a login shell, so Jonas gets Ada’s environment and lands in her home directory.
options.rationale: The dash (like `-l`) makes the new shell a login shell with the target user’s environment.

options.text: It keeps Jonas’s current directory and environment unchanged.
options.rationale: That is what plain `su ada` does; the dash gives the full login environment.

stem: On a Debian machine, which group lets its members run any command as root through `sudo`?
explanation: Which group may use `sudo` comes from `/etc/sudoers`. Debian uses the group `sudo`; Red Hat-family systems use `wheel`. Mira is in `sudo` at TuxPixel, Jonas and Ada are not.

options.text: `sudo`
options.rationale: Debian’s default sudoers file grants this group the right to run any command.

options.text: `wheel`
options.rationale: This is the administrators’ group on Red Hat-family systems, not on Debian.

options.text: `shadow`
options.rationale: The group `shadow` may read `/etc/shadow`, nothing more.

options.text: `staff`
options.rationale: On Debian this group allows writing in `/usr/local`; it does not grant root rights.

stem: Mira needs to read `/etc/shadow` once, without opening a root shell. Which command does that?
explanation: Put `sudo` in front of the command you want to run as root. To run it as someone else you add `-u NAME`; without it the target is root.

options.text: `sudo cat /etc/shadow`
options.rationale: `sudo` runs the single command `cat /etc/shadow` with root’s rights.

options.text: `su cat /etc/shadow`
options.rationale: `su` takes a user name first, so it would look for an account called `cat`.

options.text: `sudo -u jonas cat /etc/shadow`
options.rationale: `-u jonas` runs the command as Jonas, who is not allowed to read the file either.

options.text: `cat /etc/shadow | sudo`
options.rationale: `sudo` needs a command to run; piping data into it does not elevate `cat`.

stem: Ada runs `su` with no user name and a correct password. Which account does she become, and whose password did she type?
explanation: `su` switches to the account you name, root by default, and asks for **that** account’s password. This is why `sudo`, which uses your own password and logs each command, is the usual way to gain root rights.

options.text: root, and she typed her own password.
options.rationale: `su` never uses the caller’s password; that is how `sudo` works.

options.text: Jonas, the user who last logged in, and she typed his password.
options.rationale: `su` does not pick accounts from login history; the default target is root.

options.text: root, and she typed root’s password.
options.rationale: Without a name `su` means root, and it checks the target account’s password.

options.text: root, and she typed the password of the group `sudo`.
options.rationale: Groups have no password for this purpose; `su` asks for the target account’s password.

stem: Why do many administrators prefer `sudo` over sharing the root password?
explanation: The benefit of `sudo` is accountability and fine-grained control: the log shows who ran which command, and the rights of each user are set in `/etc/sudoers`.

options.text: `sudo` needs no authentication at all, so it is always faster than logging in as root and typing a password.
options.rationale: It normally asks for the caller’s own password.

options.text: Each use is logged under the real user’s name, and access can be removed per person.
options.rationale: `sudo` ties every administrative command to an individual, which a shared root password cannot do.

options.text: `sudo` gives the user a permanent root shell that survives a reboot.
options.rationale: `sudo` elevates one command at a time; nothing persists afterwards.

options.text: `sudo` encrypts every command so that other users cannot read them.
options.rationale: `sudo` does not encrypt anything; it controls and logs who may run what.

stem: Which TCP port does an SSH server listen on by default?
explanation: SSH replaced Telnet because it encrypts everything, including passwords. `sshd` listens on TCP port 22 unless an administrator changes it.

options.rationale: Port 23 is Telnet, the unencrypted predecessor of SSH.
Port 25 is used for mail transfer (SMTP).
Port 443 is HTTPS, encrypted web traffic.
SSH’s standard port is 22, and `ssh -p` is needed to use another one.

stem: Ada wants to copy `level1.txt` from her current directory to her home directory on `build.tuxpixel.example`. Which command does that?
explanation: `scp SOURCE DESTINATION` copies over SSH. A path with `user@host:` in front lives on the remote machine, so put it second to upload and first to download.

options.text: `scp level1.txt ada@build.tuxpixel.example /home/ada/`
options.rationale: Without the colon, `scp` treats the host and the path as two separate local names.

options.text: `scp level1.txt ada@build.tuxpixel.example:/home/ada/`
options.rationale: The remote side is written `user@host:path`; the local file comes first, the destination second.

options.text: `scp ada@build.tuxpixel.example:/home/ada/ level1.txt`
options.rationale: The arguments are reversed, which would try to download from the server.

options.text: `ssh level1.txt ada@build.tuxpixel.example:/home/ada/`
options.rationale: `ssh` opens a login session and does not copy files.

stem: When Mira connects to a new server for the first time and answers `yes` to the fingerprint question, where does `ssh` remember the server?
explanation: The first connection shows the server’s host key fingerprint. Once trusted, the key is saved in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`; a later change triggers a warning because someone may be impersonating the server.

options.text: In `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server.
options.rationale: That file lists the user public keys the server accepts.

options.text: In `/etc/passwd` on Mira’s own machine.
options.rationale: `/etc/passwd` is the local user database and is unrelated to SSH hosts.

options.text: In `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` on the server.
options.rationale: That is the name of a user’s public key file, not a list of servers.

options.text: In `~/.ssh/known_hosts` on Mira’s own machine.
options.rationale: The client stores the host keys of servers it has trusted in `known_hosts`.

stem: After running `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, Mira has two new files. Which one may she safely give to other people and servers?
explanation: `ssh-keygen` creates a pair: the private key (kept secret, optionally protected by a passphrase) and a public key with the same name plus `.pub`. Only the public key goes to servers.

options.text: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`
options.rationale: The `.pub` file is meant to be shared and copied into servers.

options.text: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, the private key.
options.rationale: The private key must never leave Mira’s machine.

options.text: `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, the list of trusted hosts.
options.rationale: This file is created later by `ssh`, and it is not a key pair member.

options.text: `~/.ssh/config`, the client configuration.
options.rationale: This optional file stores client settings and is not generated by `ssh-keygen`.

stem: To log in to the build server without a password, Ada adds her public key to the server. Where exactly does it go?
explanation: The server compares the key Ada presents with those in `authorized_keys` of the target account. `ssh-copy-id` appends the public key to that file for you.

options.text: A line in `~/.ssh/known_hosts` in her home directory on the server.
options.rationale: `known_hosts` is used by the client to remember servers, not to authorise users.

options.text: A line in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` in her home directory on her laptop.
options.rationale: The server decides who may log in, so the file must be on the server.

options.text: A line in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` in her home directory on the server.
options.rationale: The server accepts the keys listed in that file for the account.

options.text: A line in `/etc/shadow`, next to her password hash.
options.rationale: `/etc/shadow` stores password data; SSH keys do not go there.

stem: What is the main advantage of public key authentication over typing a password?
explanation: A key pair lets the client prove its identity without sending a secret. If the private key has a passphrase, a stolen file is also useless without it.

options.text: The public key is secret and must be hidden from the owner of the server.
options.rationale: It is the private key that is secret; the public key is meant to be shared.

options.text: The server gets to read the private key once and then caches it.
options.rationale: The private key never leaves the client.

options.text: The private key is never sent over the network, so nothing can be guessed.
options.rationale: The server only needs proof that you hold the private key, which is never sent.

options.text: It makes the connection faster because no encryption is needed.
options.rationale: The session is still encrypted; authentication does not change that.

stem: Which statements about `sudo` and `su` are true? (Choose TWO.)
explanation: `sudo` runs one command with elevated rights after checking sudoers and the caller’s password. `su` starts a shell as another user and asks for that user’s password.

options.text: `sudo` asks for the password of the user who runs it.
options.rationale: `sudo` authenticates the caller.

options.text: `su` without a name asks for root’s password.
options.rationale: The default target of `su` is root and its password is required.

options.text: `sudo` always requires the root password.
options.rationale: It uses the caller’s own password.

options.text: `su -` keeps the caller’s environment and working directory unchanged.
options.rationale: The dash requests a full login shell with the target user’s environment.

options.text: Only the account root may run `sudo`.
options.rationale: Users listed in `/etc/sudoers` or in the group `sudo` may run it.

stem: Which statements about system users on Debian are true? (Choose TWO.)
explanation: System accounts exist so services can run with limited rights. Their IDs lie below 1000 and their shell is normally `nologin`.

options.text: They usually have a shell such as `/usr/sbin/nologin`, so nobody can log in as them.
options.rationale: They exist for services, not for people.

options.text: They always have the user ID 0.
options.rationale: Only root has UID 0.

options.text: Their home directory is always `/root`.
options.rationale: Each system user has its own directory or none; `/root` belongs to root.

options.text: They must be members of the group `sudo`.
options.rationale: Most services have no administrator rights at all.

options.text: Their user IDs are normally below 1000.
options.rationale: Debian reserves 1–999 for system accounts.

stem: Mira sets up key-based logins for the build server. Which statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)
explanation: Public key authentication needs the public key on the server and the private key on the client. `ssh-keygen` creates the pair, and `known_hosts` is an unrelated client-side file.

options.text: The private key is added to `authorized_keys` so that the server can verify it.
options.rationale: A private key must never be handed to anyone.

options.text: `~/.ssh/known_hosts` on the server lists the users who may log in.
options.rationale: `known_hosts` is the client-side list of trusted servers.

options.text: A passphrase is sent to the server together with the public key.
options.rationale: A passphrase only unlocks the private key on the client.

options.text: The public key is appended to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` of the account on the server.
options.rationale: The server reads that file to learn which keys may log in.

options.text: The private key stays on Mira’s machine and is never copied to the server.
options.rationale: Only the public half needs to be shared.

stem: Mira needs a new Ed25519 key pair for logins to the build server. Type the command that generates it, naming the key type.
explanation: `ssh-keygen -t TYPE` creates a key pair; Ed25519 is the type OpenSSH uses by default.

stem: The build server’s SSH daemon listens on port 2222. Type the command that connects as `ada` to `build.tuxpixel.example` on that port.
explanation: Lower-case `-p` gives `ssh` the port. (`scp` uses a capital `-P` instead.) The user can be given as `user@host` or with `-l`.

stem: Type the path, starting from the home directory, of the file in which the server lists the public keys allowed to log in to that account.
explanation: Each account’s `authorized_keys` file sits in its `.ssh` directory; sshd ignores it if the permissions are too open.

stem: Type the command that prints your user ID, your group ID and your supplementary groups, with both numbers and names.
explanation: `id` prints `uid=… gid=… groups=…`. Options such as `-u`, `-g` and `-G` show single parts, and `-n` swaps numbers for names.

stem: Mira runs a command in the studio’s terminal. What does it print?
explanation: `id -u` prints only the numeric user ID. Standard users start at 1000 on Debian; Mira, the first one, got 1000.

options.rationale: Mira is the first standard user on the machine, so her UID is 1000.
UID 0 belongs to root; Mira works as a standard user.
27 is the group ID of `sudo`, not her user ID.
1001 is Jonas’s user ID.

stem: What does this command print for the system account `daemon`? (Fields: UID, then login shell.)
explanation: `getent passwd NAME` prints the account’s /etc/passwd line, and `cut` picks fields 3 (UID) and 7 (shell). System users have low IDs and `/usr/sbin/nologin`.

options.text: 1000:/bin/bash
options.rationale: That would be a standard user such as Mira.

options.text: 0:/usr/sbin/nologin
options.rationale: UID 0 is root; `daemon` has a different, low ID.

options.text: 1:/bin/bash
options.rationale: The UID is right for a system user, but a service account does not get a login shell.

options.text: 1:/usr/sbin/nologin
options.rationale: A system user has a UID far below 1000 and `nologin` as its shell.

stem: In the format owner, group, octal mode, what does this command print for the file holding the password hashes?
explanation: Only root can write `/etc/shadow`, and only root and the group `shadow` can read it (mode 640), so standard users cannot see the hashes.
